summary: Terminator is a web tool for quickly comparing lunar landing sites and dates by the two things a lander needs: sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for direct communication. Pick any of 9 curated sites (Apollo 11 and 17, Clavius, Chang’e 4, Chandrayaan-3, and four south pole sites including Shackleton and Malapert) and a date between Nov 2026 and Dec 2028. It shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the horizon, how long until sunset or Earthset, a 30-day timeline of power and comms windows, and a side-by-side comparison of two sites. Positions come from NASA/JPL Horizons. For five south-polar sites it also uses real NASA LOLA terrain: a flat horizon says each gets about 50% sunlight, but the Shackleton ridge is actually lit 92% of the time while Haworth crater’s floor gets none. That’s why small changes in landing site matter so much at the pole.
details:
What it does. Terminator is a web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates by the two things a lander needs most: sunlight for solar power, and a line of sight to Earth for direct communication. You pick a site and a date (Nov 2026 – Dec 2028), and it shows where the Sun and Earth are in that site’s sky, whether terrain blocks them, how long until sunset or Earthset, a 30-day timeline of power and comms windows, and a side-by-side comparison of two sites. A strip at the top shows all 9 sites at once, so you can compare them at a glance.

How it works. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons, queried hourly for each site as a surface observer on the Moon. For the 5 south-polar sites, I computed a real terrain skyline from the LRO LOLA south-pole elevation map (240 m/pixel): from a point 2 m above the ground, the script looks in 720 directions out to 250 km, keeps the highest terrain angle in each direction, and accounts for the Moon’s curvature. A body counts as visible only if it is above the skyline in its own direction. Everything is precomputed, so the site loads instantly and never depends on a live API.

Why it matters. At the south pole the Sun never rises more than a few degrees, so a ridge kilometres away decides everything. A flat-horizon calculation says every polar site gets about 50% sunlight. Real terrain says otherwise: the Shackleton ridge crest is lit 92% of the time, while Haworth crater’s floor, about 80 km away, gets 0% sunlight and never sees Earth. That is a permanently shadowed region, which matches what is known about it. Terminator makes that difference visible in seconds, for mission planners re-evaluating sites when schedules slip, and for students and the public curious why the lunar south pole is so hard.

Validation. The maximum Sun elevation at each site matches 90° − |latitude| + 1.54°. A synthetic-mountain test placed the skyline peak at the correct direction and angle. A check on Shackleton crater confirmed the map is not mirrored. Shackleton and Malapert were snapped to their real LOLA high points.

Limitations. 240 m terrain can miss small slopes, the Sun is treated as a point, only polar sites use terrain, and custom coordinates are not supported yet.

Tools. Python (requests, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj), plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript with hand-drawn SVG charts, hosted on GitHub Pages. Code: github.com/Acookiefor2/lunar-sites
